newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Solana secures place in NATO history.
newsitem.headline: Solana secures place in NATO history.

text.p: By negotiating a landmark NATO-Russia pact, alliance Secretary-General Javier Solana has secured himself a place in the history of an organisation whose very existence he once opposed.
"He played a decisive role. He kept the allies together," one NATO ambassador said after news of the breakthrough with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov reached Brussels.

Solana, 54, was mandated last December to try to negotiate the deal with Russia to establish a central plank of a new European security order and overcome Moscow's fears over NATO's planned eastwards enlargement.
Before a furious Russian propaganda onslaught, he kept his nerve -- making clear NATO wanted a deal with Moscow, but enlargement would take place anyway.

Through six rounds of hard negotiating, Solana maintained alliance solidarity and rejected Russian pressure for limits on the freedom of action act of likely new members, such as Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic.
"There is no doubt, this is a personal triumph. It is good for Solana, good for NATO, good for the Russians and good for the new members," said one alliance source.

Solana, a former Spanish foreign minister with a track record as a tough negotiator, was up against a formidable adversary in Primakov -- an ex-Kremlin spy-master and hardened veteran of arms control talks with the West.
"He had to make Russia understand it stood to gain more by signing than not signing," added the source.
The deal with Russia caps a frantic period for Solana who took over as the NATO head in December 1995 after Belgium's Willy Claes was forced to resign in a local bribery scandal.

The appointment brought much prestige to Spain, a country not fully integrated into all of NATO's military structures, and was seen as a sign of how the alliance was transforming itself from Cold War military machine to a European-wide security body.

Solana immediately won plaudits for his skilful handling of the weekly meetings of NATO's 16 ambassadors -- the alliance's policy-making forum -- and negotiations with Bosnian Serb leaders over the implementation of the Dayton peace accords.
His relaxed, warm personal style -- in sharp contrast to Claes' bad-tempered outbursts -- pleased both staff and visitors while hard work and professionalism won over more admirers.

Solana, a married man with two children, travelled widely both to NATO members and non-members using to good effect all the contacts he had made while president of the European Union's Council of Ministers.
He frequently visited former Yugoslavia where NATO troops police the Dayton peace accords which ended the 3-1/2 year Bosnian war and became the first NATO head to visit Moscow for almost five years.

Insiders say the personal rapport he established with NATO's leaders saw him entrusted with the task of negotiating the deal with Primakov. Previous major East-West accords have usually seen key NATO capitals taking the lead in the negotiations.
A physicist by education, Solana had as a young socialist militant opposed Spain's NATO membership.

Staff say Solana -- a keen sportsmen -- likes to joke his punishing work routine reflects a northern European approach in the morning when he starts work early and a southern European approach in the evening when he finishes late.
